summary: 5-week-old first-born boy (3.6 kg), 6 days of projectile non-bilious vomiting after every feed, hungry afterwards, weight static; olive palpable; VBG pH 7.53, HCO3 36, Cl 86, K 3.0. Correct fluids and electrolytes first; pyloromyotomy is not an emergency.

inputs.hpi: 5-week-old first-born boy, birth weight 3.5 kg. Six days of forceful projectile vomiting of milk (never green) shortly after every feed, then immediately hungry again. Fewer wet nappies, weight has not increased. No diarrhoea, no fever.

exam.general: Alert, hungry. Mildly sunken fontanelle, dry mucosa. T 36.9, HR 150, CRT 2 s.
exam.abdomen: Visible gastric peristalsis; firm olive-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant during a test feed.

confirmedDiagnosis.name: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
confirmedDiagnosis.assessmentText: Clinical pyloric stenosis (palpable olive) with hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Confirm with pyloric ultrasound; NBM, IV fluids with potassium to correct alkalosis and chloride before surgery; paediatric surgery for pyloromyotomy once corrected.

socratesAnswers.associated: Projectile vomiting after feeds, hungry after, fewer wet nappies

mustNotMiss.knownGapNote: PANE has no pyloric stenosis disease node (pane-engine has 130 diseases, none for pyloric stenosis); top 3: inguinal/femoral hernia, acute cholecystitis, appendicitis. Q40.0 maps to no protocol. Symptom inference ranks hypertrophic pyloric stenosis #1 (secondary view, its investigations are not surfaced).
mustNotMiss.proposedFix: Add paediatric surgical conditions (intussusception, pyloric stenosis, malrotation/volvulus) as PANE nodes and management protocols (Q40.0, Q43.3, K56.1) with paediatric surgery referral.

emergencyLevel.note: Dehydrated infant: same-day admission. Surgery itself is not an emergency.

mustInclude.note: Chloride and bicarbonate (blood gas) define the alkalosis that must be corrected before anaesthesia; a generic pre-operative U&E does not count.
Anaesthesia with uncorrected alkalosis risks post-operative apnoea: correct fluids and electrolytes first.

mustExclude.note: Weight 3.6 kg. Paracetamol 1 g, ibuprofen 400 mg, piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g, co-amoxiclav 1.2 g, meropenem 1 g, morphine 2.5–5 mg, ondansetron 4 mg and fixed 1 L, 1–2 L or 500 mL fluid volumes are adult fixed doses; a child needs weight-based (mg/kg, mL/kg) dosing. Prescribing accuracy is a patient-safety issue, so critical.
Pyloromyotomy is scheduled after resuscitation, not as an emergency.

An ACS, PE or AF antithrombotic/thrombolytic plan must never be attached to this diagnosis. guideline.name: Pyloric stenosis in pediatric surgery — an evidence-based review
guideline.section: Pyloromyotomy is not an emergency: correct dehydration and hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis before anaesthesia; ultrasound diagnosis; laparoscopic or open pyloromyotomy
guideline.citation: Pandya S, Heiss K. Pyloric stenosis in pediatric surgery: an evidence-based review. Surg Clin North Am. 2012;92:527–539.

guideline.name: ACR Appropriateness Criteria — vomiting in infants
guideline.section: Non-bilious projectile vomiting (suspected hypertrophic pyloric stenosis): ultrasound of the pylorus; bilious vomiting in an infant: upper GI contrast series (malrotation/midgut volvulus) as a surgical emergency
guideline.citation: Expert Panel on Pediatric Imaging; Alazraki AL, Rigsby CK, Iyer RS, et al. ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Vomiting in Infants. J Am Coll Radiol. 2020;17:S505–S515.

rationale: Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency (dehydration, alkalosis) but a surgical non-emergency. Ultrasound confirms; fluids and electrolytes are corrected before pyloromyotomy.
